rashi:a1.1: The [new] moon would come early: the new moon would arrive three days before Rosh HaShana, so that the molad is on Wednesday and Rosh HaShana on Shabbat; and people would mutter against the Rabbis, saying: They do whatever they want.
gershom:a1.1: If so, the moon would come early: the molad of the moon of Tishrei [would arrive] three days before Rosh HaShana. How so? A lunar month is never less than twenty-nine and a half days and 793 parts. When we make the months one of 29 and one of 30, the molad always evens out over two months, since the half day of the thirty-day month is taken and given to the twenty-nine-day one. When they are all in their order, the molad of Tishrei comes on time, on Rosh HaShana. But if they make nine full, six half days are left over, that is, three days, which cannot be given to deficient months, and the molad [of Tishrei] comes three days before Rosh HaShana.
gershom:a2.1: Now too: when there are eight full, there are four more full than deficient, and [the moon] comes early [also] by two days.
rashi:a2.1: As Rav Mesharshiyya says: below, regarding Shavuot (9b): for example, where it was a leap year. Here too: for example, where the year before it was a leap year.
rashi:a2.2: The intercalation of the year is a month: it is in our hands to make the month added to the year either full or deficient. We made last year’s added month deficient, so it turns out that we brought last Tishrei ahead of its molad by the measure of one month’s deficiency. Therefore we can delay this Tishrei by the measure of one month’s fullness, as it says: Remove a full month against the deficient one.
tosafot:a2.1: Here too, for example, where the year before it was a leap year: [one might object:] we are dealing with that very year, so he should have said that this year is a leap year, and that is why we make eight full. “Here too, where the year before it was a leap year” means: this year, in which we made eight full [months, is the year before the Rosh HaShana in question]. Had there been no intercalation, then if last year the fixing [of Rosh HaShana] and the molad were on Shabbat, this year’s fixing, with the months in their order, would be on Wednesday (on which the molad falls), and when full months are added it is delayed another day, up to the seventh day. [But with the intercalation,] the molad fell on Thursday at 21 hours and was not seen until Friday; so it is early by only one day.
gershom:a3.1: As Rav Mesharshiyya says: below, regarding Shavuot: for example, where it was a leap [year], etc. And last year’s intercalation was twenty-nine days: remove from these four full months one full month against that deficient one, namely the added month (the added month being deficient).
rashi:a2.3: And still one day: even though it is a day and a half, he calls it one day. And the same would hold if this year itself were a leap year: he could also have answered that it is seen fit to make eight months full. The reason he chose the year before it is that the mishna cannot be set in a leap year. It teaches “no fewer than four full months,” implying that four full months suffice; in a leap year that would leave nine deficient. And both according to Rav Huna and according to Ulla, even eight deficient can be set only in a leap year, but nine, neither in an ordinary year nor in a leap year, as below.
rashi:a2.4: People do not pay attention: over one day they do not wonder and do not mutter.
tosafot:a2.2: People do not pay attention to one day: this implies that nowadays too we make eight full months where [the moon] is early by only one day. And there is a difficulty: nowadays we postpone [Rosh HaShana when the molad falls at] GaTRaD [Tuesday, 9 hours, 204 parts], because the following year it would be on the seventh day at 18 hours and be fixed on Monday, so there are six days, and two months are made full, and still there is only one day. One must say that those who arranged the intercalations and fixings for us did not want to institute that a year should ever be lengthened by more than seven full months.
gershom:a4.1: Still there is one day: a whole one and more [the moon comes one day early]. People do not pay attention to one day: since right after [the moon] is seen it is covered, and they do not realize that it was not yet the molad.
rashi:a4.1: The moon would lag: the old [moon would linger] three days after Rosh HaShana. For the order of the months follows the moon’s molad, one full and one deficient, as I explained; and when you make three more deficient, you bring Rosh HaShana three days ahead of it.
tosafot:a4.1: Why not nine deficient: because if so the moon would lag three days. With the months in their order, the fixing would fall on the day of the molad, on Wednesday; because of three [extra] deficient months three days are taken off, and it would be fixed on Sunday. With two as well, it lags two days, and it would be fixed on Monday.
gershom:a5.1: [For if we made nine deficient, the moon would lag three days: because of the three days of the six [extra] deficient [half days] taken from the days of the moon, the molad would be delayed in coming until three days after Rosh HaShana.
gershom:a6.1: Now too: when there are eight deficient, it lags two days, because of these four deficient that are more than the full ones.
rashi:a5.1: Where the year before it: last year, was a leap year and the added month was thirty days, while by the count of the moon it is only twenty-nine and a half. It turns out that it delays Rosh HaShana by half a day, and now [the gap] from Rosh HaShana is only a day and a half. Since these are not two whole days, he counts it as one; and that is why he asks: And still there is one day.
tosafot:a5.1: In brief: Where the year before it was a leap year and the added month was thirty: the fixing would have been due on Monday because of the eight deficient; now, because of the thirty-day added month, it is delayed two more days, to Wednesday, while the molad is on Thursday at 21 hours. That is why he asks: there is still one day. Question: there are really two days, since [the new moon] stays hidden for six hours and will not be seen until Friday. Answer: it speaks where last year’s molad was five hours into the day before the fixing; adding five days, 21 hours and 589 parts, the molad is nine hours into the day and can be seen on Thursday by those in the Land of Israel, so it is only one day off. But if last year’s molad was at the start of Shabbat, so that this year it is Thursday at 21 hours and is not seen that day, we would certainly not make eight deficient, for then the moon would lag two days. Question: granted that Rav Huna explains the latter clause, “it did not seem appropriate to make more than eight full,” so eight full we do make, found only in a leap year; but on the first clause, “no fewer than four full months,” he must explain like Ulla that we do not make more than eight deficient, so eight we do make, namely where [the moon] is seen on Thursday itself because last year the molad preceded the fixing. Then the mishna speaks of two different cases. Answer: the tanna of the mishna came to teach every way we can change the months from their order: the first clause teaches that we make eight deficient if last year the molad preceded the fixing, and the latter clause that we make eight full if it did not. And by what I explained above, both clauses are set in the same kind of case. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a7.1: The intercalation of the year was thirty: take now the fullness of the added month and give it to one of the deficient ones; there is still one day of deficiency, and the moon lags. They assume, etc.
rashi:a6.1: It was surely seen: the moon, by the court; and it is we who did not take the trouble to look out and see it. Therefore they do not mutter.
rashi:b1.1: With regard to what do they disagree: Rav Huna, who sets the mishna as two separate matters, holds like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, that [the added month is] sometimes 29 and sometimes thirty [Rashi takes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s “a month” as either length; the Davidson English renders it as a deficient month of twenty-nine days]. The mishna is then explained thus: “No fewer than four full months”: we do not make more than eight deficient, but eight deficient we do make, and that is found only in a leap year whose added month is thirty, as Ulla [explained]. “And it did not seem appropriate to make more than eight full”: but eight full we do make, in a leap year whose added month is 29, as above; and that is according to Rabban Shimon. Ulla holds like the first tanna, that it is always thirty. Therefore [for him] the mishna can be set only as one statement: it teaches “it did not seem appropriate to make more than eight deficient,” but eight we do make, in a leap year whose added month is thirty; but full months, not even eight do we make, since the moon would come two days early. For a leap year whose added month is 29 cannot be set up as Rav Huna does, since the added month of a year is never less than thirty.
gershom:b1.1: With regard to what do they disagree: Rav Huna and Ulla. Rav Huna is like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
rashi:b2.1: Only on the day of waving: on the same day [of the week] on which the sixteenth of Nisan fell. For on the sixteenth of Nisan we begin to count fifty, and the fiftieth day falls on the [weekday of the] first day of the count, since day forty-nine is the end of the seventh week, and on day fifty the [next] week begins.
gershom:b2.1: Shavuot falls only on the day of waving: on the day the omer is waved, of which it is written: “On the morrow after the Sabbath the priest shall wave it.”
rashi:b2.2: And Rosh HaShana only… or on the night after its extra day [le’or ibburo]: the night after the extra day of Nisan, on the day [of the week] on which the thirty-first of Nisan fell. For example, if Nisan [began] on Sunday, the night after its extra day is Tuesday. It is called “the night after its extra day” because that is the night on which the month is made extended: when they make Rosh Ḥodesh on day thirty-one, the past month is full.
gershom:b3.1: [Always, from the day of waving until Shavuot there are 49 days, that is, seven weeks, and at the start of the eighth week is Shavuot, day fifty; and that fiftieth day falls on the [weekday of the] day of waving.] Or on the night after its extra day: on the morrow [of the day of waving], on the night after the day of waving has passed.
gershom:b4.1: And some say: the night after its extra day [of Nisan], that is, day thirty-one, and that thirty-first day falls on the [weekday of the] day after the day of waving.
rashi:b3.1: Both deficient: Kislev and Sivan. Since there are then four deficient in the winter and four deficient in the summer, Rosh HaShana falls on the day of waving. For nowadays we always make the summer months in their order, and we have a fixed mnemonic, At-Bash, G–R: [Rosh HaShana falls on the weekday of] the third day of Passover, that is, the night after its extra day [the first day of Passover falls on the weekday of Tisha B’Av, the second on Shavuot, the third on Rosh HaShana]. When one more is made deficient, it brings Rosh HaShana one day earlier, to the day of waving. But according to Rav Huna, who says we also make full months: once we make four full in the summer, it delays Rosh HaShana one day, so that it falls on the night after the night after the extra day of Nisan, the fourth day of Passover.
tosafot:b3.1: Two deficient, on the day of waving: the sixteenth of Nisan. One full and one deficient, on the night after its extra day: meaning the night after its extra day, that is, day thirty-one; for the thirty-first of Nisan is on the same day [of the week] on which the seventeenth of Nisan fell, which is the third day of Passover.
gershom:b5.1: Both deficient: Iyar and Sivan; [then Rosh HaShana falls] on the day of waving.
gershom:b6.1: For if we make eight deficient, we make four in the winter, Marḥeshvan and Kislev and Tevet and Adar, [and four in the summer: Iyar and Sivan corresponding to Marḥeshvan and Kislev, Tammuz and Elul corresponding to Tevet and Adar]. When it says “both deficient,” it means [read: Adar] and Sivan, because they are not usually both deficient every year; and then Rosh HaShana falls on the [day of waving]. How so? If Rosh Ḥodesh Nisan was on Shabbat, the day of waving, the sixteenth, is on Sunday. Rosh Ḥodesh Iyar is on Sunday and Monday, Rosh Ḥodesh Sivan on Tuesday, Tammuz on Wednesday, Av on Thursday, Elul on Friday and Shabbat, since Av was full; so Rosh HaShana falls on [Sunday], which is the day of waving.
gershom:b7.1: One full and one deficient, on the night after its extra day: because one day is left over [since the third month is full]. But sometimes you find Rosh HaShana on the night after the night after its extra day, on the third day after the waving. How so? Because once we say four full, yet another day is left over.
rashi:b6.1: But seven we do make: even according to Ulla. The reason we do not make eight full is that the moon would come two days early; but seven, where it comes only one day early, we do make. And sometimes we do not do it in the winter, making the winter months in their order, and we extend in the summer and make four full; and then it would also be on the night after the night after its extra day.
gershom:b8.1: It is eight full that we do not make, but seven full we do make: sometimes they do not make the fourth in the winter, making only three full in the winter, and they make four full in the summer, and it falls on the night after the night after its extra day, as we said above.]
rashi:b7.1: Rather: this baraita, which teaches always “the night after its extra day” and no later, is Aḥerim, who do not hold of [extra] full and deficient months, since for them all the months are always in their order.
gershom:b9.1: Rather, whose is this baraita, which says that Rosh HaShana falls only on the day of waving or on the night after its extra day?
rashi:b7.2: Only four days: if Rosh HaShana fell on Sunday, next year it comes on Thursday; that is when they are all in their order.
gershom:b10.1: It is Aḥerim: who hold that it is always one full and one deficient, making 354 days. Three hundred and fifty of them come out in sevens, leaving four days, and these are what lies between one Rosh HaShana and the next. And if it was [a leap year], five: this follows the one who says the added month of a year is a month of 29 days, which leaves one day over the weeks. But according to the one who says the added month is thirty, two days are left, and there would be six days between one Rosh HaShana and the next. Aḥerim say five because fewer than five is impossible according to everyone.
rashi:b8.1: On the day of waving you do not find it: for in the regular order it falls on the night after its extra day.
tosafot:b8.1: Ultimately, according to Aḥerim you do not find it on the day of waving, etc.: [the answer is:] for example, where it was a leap year whose added month was thirty. Since we made the added month thirty days, we must make one of the summer’s full months deficient; thus we find it on the day of waving.
gershom:b11.1: [Ultimately, according to Aḥerim you do find the night after its extra day, since they hold the regular order, and we said above: one full and one deficient, the night after its extra day. But the day of waving, according to Aḥerim, you do not find.]
gershom:b12.1: For example, where it was a leap year and the added month was thirty, remove a month against a month: that is, since the first Adar is full, you must make Nisan deficient against it. For the deficiency of the second Adar corresponds to Av, which is full; therefore you must make Nisan deficient because of the first Adar, which is full. Now there are four deficient in the summer, and so Rosh HaShana falls on the day of waving [as we answered above: both deficient, on the day of waving].
rashi:b9.1: Remove a month: of the summer, and make it deficient against the added month that you made full. Just as we make Shevat and the first Adar full together, we also make Nisan and Iyar deficient together, since we say “and if it was a leap year, five.” Since the added month is thirty, if we did not make two deficient together, there would be six [days] between one Rosh HaShana and the next, because when you add one full month to the months of the year it delays Rosh HaShana two days. Therefore there are four deficient in the summer, and it falls on the day of waving.
rashi:b10.1: Did Aḥerim come to teach us the count? This is said in astonishment. Since they hold of the regular order, it is obvious that there are only four between one and the next. They should rather have said: one does not extend a month [to thirty days] for convenience, and I would know on my own that there are only four between them.
gershom:b13.1: Did Aḥerim come to teach us the count? That is: let them say that [the months] are always in their order, and we would know on our own that between one Rosh HaShana and the next, etc.
rashi:b10.2: [This teaches us]: had they said “one does not extend the month for convenience,” I would have said that this applies to a month [whose moon] was seen on time; but where witnesses did not come on day thirty, you must extend it, since it is a mitzva to sanctify by witnesses.
rashi:b10.3: It teaches us, etc.: for this is what it implies: hold on to this sign, four days between one and the next, even if the moon was not seen.
gershom:b14.1: This teaches us that we do not need [to consider it] a mitzva to sanctify by sighting: to wait until witnesses come. Rather, we follow the calculation, and between one Rosh HaShana and the next there is always, etc.
rashi:b11.1: But there is the day of hours: that is, granted that Aḥerim follow the moon’s moladot, still there are sometimes five days in an ordinary year between one Passover and the next, because of the day of hours: every three years one extra day accumulates. For between one molad and that of the next year there are four days, eight hours and 876 parts; take three years at eight hours a year and you will find one day.
rashi:b11.2: And the day of thirty years: for of the 876 [parts], take 864 from each 876 and you will find a day in thirty years. There are 1,080 parts in an hour; count five times 864 as four hours; so in thirty years, 864 [a year] make 24 hours, which is one day.
gershom:b15.1: [But according to Aḥerim there is the day of hours: two-thirds of an hour in each month add up to eight hours [a year], and in three years those hours add up to a day. And 73 parts in each month add up to 876 parts a year; take twelve parts from them and 864 remain, and in thirty years the 864 make one day; that is “and the day of thirty years.”
rashi:b12.1: And Shmuel too holds like Rav Huna: that we also make eight full.
rashi:b13.1: Both full: [if] two of the deficient [months], such as Marḥeshvan and Iyar, you make full, the year comes out two days over the regular order, and that is 356.
rashi:b13.2: Both deficient: [if] two of the full ones, such as Kislev and Sivan, you make deficient, the year comes out two days short of the regular order, and that is 352; and in their order, 354. Evidently we make eight full.
gershom:b16.1: How so? Both full: Marḥeshvan and Iyar, 356. Since we say that when there are six full and six deficient the year is 354 days, learn from it that when there are eight full the year is 356 days, and if there are eight deficient it is 352. Evidently Shmuel holds that one makes both eight full and eight deficient, [like Rav Huna]; but Ulla does not hold that one makes eight full at all.
rashi:b14.1: I am hereby a nazirite like the days of the sun: or that he said “like the number of the days of the sun”: he counts 365 [days of] naziriteship.
gershom:b17.1: I am hereby a nazirite: [as if he said:] I take upon myself naziriteships of thirty days, like an ordinary naziriteship; he counts 365 naziriteships, like the number of the days of the sun, by the reckoning of four seasons, four times 91 days and seven and a half hours, which is 365 days. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads this as 365 separate terms of naziriteship; the Davidson English renders it as a single term of 365 days.]
gershom:b18.1: 354 days: that is when there is one full and one deficient. And if so, you find [a year of] 356 when both are full.] And the new moon was seen in its time [on Rosh HaShana]: and this disagrees with Ulla, who says one does not make more than eight deficient.
rashi:b16.1: And Rabbi too holds like Rav Huna: who says we make eight full.
rashi:b16.2: And the new moon was seen: the moon of Tishrei, in its time, on the day Rosh HaShana was fixed.
rashi:b16.3: And Rabbi was astonished: because it should have lagged three days after the moon, since they had brought the fixing three days forward.
tosafot:b16.1: In brief: Rabbi made nine deficient and the new moon was seen in its time, that is, the molad of Tishrei on the day the year was fixed. Rabbi wondered how, with nine deficient, it could be seen on time: he assumed that last year’s fixing and molad were on Shabbat; he made nine deficient, and the year was fixed on Sunday; so by right [the new moon] should not have come until Wednesday, three days after the fixing. His son Rabbi Shimon answered: perhaps it was a leap year, the added month was thirty, and last year we made both full; remove three against three and it is back in its place. That is: this year, in which the nine deficient were made, was a leap year; last year’s fixing was indeed on Shabbat; because this year had a thirty-day added month, its fixing should have come six days after last year’s, on Wednesday, and because Rabbi made three [extra] deficient it was fixed on Sunday. Last year two were made full, so last year’s molad preceded the fixing by two days and fell on Tuesday; adding five days, 21 hours and 589 parts, this year’s molad is on Sunday, and it was seen on the day of the fixing. Difficulty: if last year’s molad was on Tuesday, two days before the fixing, how did they make eight full? Above we concluded that we make eight full only when that year is a leap year and [the moon] is early by only one day. And if last year’s molad was Tuesday after 18 hours and not seen until Wednesday, then this year’s molad is Monday at 15 hours, while the fixing was on Sunday, so how was it seen on time? Even if last year’s molad was Tuesday at six hours (not seen in Babylonia until Wednesday), this year’s is Monday at 3 hours, still not on time. Perhaps “seen in its time” is not exact: the day after the fixing is also called its time, since a molad one day after the fixing does not matter, as people do not pay attention; so a molad on the day after the fixing counts as on the day of the fixing.
